newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia, U.S. differ on progress of NATO talks.
newsitem.headline: Russia, U.S. differ on progress of NATO talks.

text.p: The United States said on Friday it had made progress in talks with Russia on NATO expansion, but Moscow was more cautious in its assessment, insisting it was too early to talk of any breakthrough.

In the Russian parliament, deputies urged a ban on foreign investment in key areas in a move that smacked of communist unease over Western economic influence. But analysts said their action would have little impact.
U.S. optimism came from Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, who finished a two-day visit by meeting Russian President Boris Yeltsin in the Kremlin.

"I think that we have made some very important progress on this," she told a news conference, referring to a document that would define a new relationship between NATO and Russia as the alliance expands eastwards.
She added: "We are no longer in a situation of you versus us. We are all on the same side... The new NATO is not the NATO of the Cold War."
Albright said Yeltsin, who has been ill for most of the last eight months, was clearly in control, although reporters said he looked pale and waxen when he met the U.S. diplomat.
Russia has staunchly opposed plans by the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation to invite several one-time members of the Soviet-era Warsaw Pact to join the alliance.
But Russian officials were more reserved in describing the talks on NATO's eastwards.
"It's premature to talk about a breakthrough," Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky told a news briefing. "I would rather say one can express cautious optimism."
Yastrzhembsky said Russia sought a strong deal with NATO which would guarantee its security interests.

As though to underscore the traditional differences between Moscow and the West, Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, who met Albright on Thursday evening, on Friday visited the headquarters of Russia's nuclear missile forces.
"Russian strategic missile forces are capable of effectively carrying out all tasks entrusted to them," Interfax quoted him as saying after visiting the headquarters outside Moscow.
Defence officials have expressed fears that Russia's cash-strapped military might soon be unable to control its missiles or to respond adequately to military threats.
Also on Friday, the Duma, the lower house of parliament, attempted to make it harder for foreigners to invest in Russia.

Deputies in the communist-dominated State Duma voted 261 to 10 in a first reading to ban foreign activity in some areas involving national security such as power supplies and telecoms, and limit it in others, such as oil and financial services.
But analysts said the vote would have little impact.
"There are lots of people...that say crazy things," said Bill Browder, managing director of Hermitage Capital Management equity fund in Moscow.
"But the government policy is generally open to investment and I do not expect that to change."
The Communist Party says there is a danger foreigners will buy up Russian industry on the cheap.
"This law is just what is needed to stop the fragmentation of the country," senior Communist Party deputy Anatoly Lukyanov told the house during the debate.
